# Discussion

## Interpretation of our Findings

For each target variable, two feature representations were compared:
raw, in which plant-derived features enter the model on their original
absolute scale, and session_norm, in which each feature is expressed as
a robust z-score relative to the median and spread of its respective
recording session. This distinction addresses a key property of the
sensing setup: as described in Section 5.1.1, the DC level of the plant
voltage drifts between sessions due to factors such as ambient
temperature and room-level CO~2~ baseline. These factors are unrelated
to emotional state but can shift the absolute voltage range across
sessions.

Since each session corresponds to exactly one participant, a classifier
trained on raw voltage levels could implicitly associate specific
voltage ranges with specific participants, rather than learning a
genuine relationship between signal dynamics and emotional state. This
constitutes a form of session-level leakage that may inflate apparent
performance without reflecting true predictive signal. Session
normalization mitigates this issue by removing session-identity
information and re-expressing each feature relative to its
session-specific center and spread prior to training.

The results support this interpretation. For valence, session
normalization increased the average macro-F1 score across all three
classifiers by 0.031, with the largest gain observed for Random Forest
(+0.068). For arousal, the average macro-F1 score improved by 0.035. In
both cases, the best-performing models used session-normalized
features.

Emotion classification (Section 5.1.3) is the only case in which this
pattern did not hold: Random Forest performed slightly better on raw
features (0.21) than on session-normalized features (0.19). However,
this difference is small relative to the overall variation across all
six model-feature combinations (macro-F1 approximately 0.18-0.21). It is
therefore
more likely attributable to performance variability among similarly
performing models than to a failure of session normalization for this
target variable.

Arousal remained the weakest target variable overall, with performance
close to chance and the best result narrowly missing statistical
significance (p = 0.0547). This is consistent with a methodological
limitation already noted in Section 6.4: the arousal axis relies
exclusively on RMSSD and mean heart rate, and @choi2017's work suggests
these markers are reliable indicators of emotional state only for
unpleasant, highly arousing stimuli, not for neutral or pleasant ones.
Since the video stimulus combines strongly negative segments with
comparatively mild or neutral ones, only part of the recorded material
may fall within the range where HRV is expected to track arousal at
all, independently of any limitation in the plant signal itself.

The correlation analysis (Section 5.2) complements these findings. While
CO~2~ showed substantial correlations with plant features in the raw
analysis, these associations decreased markedly after removing
between-session variance. This suggests that most of the observed
plant-CO~2~ coupling reflects slow session-level drift rather than
within-session physiological interaction. Importantly, the
plant-valence relationship remained stable under CO~2~ control at both
levels, indicating that this association is not an artifact of shared
environmental influences.

## Comparison with Previous Studies

The present study directly addresses the two central limitations that
@gloor2025 explicitly identified: the lack of a standardized elicitation
protocol and the single-subject design. By employing a fixed, ten-minute
video stimulus instead of post-hoc labeling of unconstrained behaviour,
and by recording 15 participants with grouped cross-validation to
prevent participant-level leakage, the present study constitutes a
multi-participant replication of this experimental paradigm with a
controlled emotion-elicitation protocol.

The shift from a binary "happy"/"sad" classification to a dimensional
valence-arousal framework [@russell1980] further extends this
replication methodologically: it allows for a more fine-grained analysis
than Gloor's binary scheme permitted, and reveals that plant signals are
informative for valence but not for arousal — a distinction that could
not have been captured within a binary classification framework in the
first place (see Section 5.1.1).

Both studies validate their findings via permutation testing, supporting
the conclusion that the reported results in either case are unlikely to
be driven by data leakage. However, a direct comparison of raw accuracy
values (72.8-73.8% in @gloor2025 versus 36-43% in the present study) is
complicated by differences in class distribution and evaluation
metrics: @gloor2025 report accuracy figures from an imbalanced (60/40)
classification task without a macro-F1 or comparable metric. As
discussed in Section 5.1.3, accuracy alone may overestimate performance
when classifiers favor the majority class, making it difficult to assess
to what extent the accuracy reported by @gloor2025 reflects genuinely
balanced discriminative performance rather than class-imbalance effects.
This limits the comparability of the two accuracy figures beyond a
coarse indication that both are above chance level.

## Implications for the Academic Literature / Future Research

First, the comparison with @gloor2025 suggests that the lower accuracy
observed in the present study is more plausibly attributable to a more
conservative and generalizable evaluation framework than to a weaker
underlying effect. In particular, grouped cross-validation across 15
participants and permutation testing were used to mitigate
session-specific leakage that a single-subject design cannot address.
Future studies should therefore build on these findings by using larger
and more diverse participant samples to reduce the wide confidence
intervals observed for arousal and emotion classification. Ideally, such
studies should also be conducted under professionally controlled
laboratory conditions, with stable air quality, humidity, and
temperature, in order to minimize the session-level environmental drift
identified in Section 5.2 and to isolate the physiological signal of
interest more effectively.

Second, operationalizing emotion via the dimensional valence-arousal
model [@russell1980] revealed differential sensitivity across affective
dimensions that would likely have remained obscured under a combined
categorical label. This indicates that valence and arousal should be
treated as analytically distinct constructs in this line of research.
Future work should therefore model valence and arousal as separate
targets and incorporate dimension-specific refinements. For example,
alternative HRV-based markers for arousal could be evaluated beyond
RMSSD, given its documented limitations at lower arousal levels
[@choi2017], and higher-performing FER models than HSEmotion could be
tested for the valence dimension. Complementing physiological measures
with validated self-report instruments such as the Self-Assessment
Manikin [@bradleylang1994] may further strengthen interpretation,
provided that such measures are used in addition to, rather than instead
of, the physiological channels employed here.

Third, the correlation analysis identified an additional methodological
issue that has received little attention in research on plant
bioelectrical signals: environmental variables such as CO~2~ should be
recorded explicitly and controlled statistically, as the present
analysis indicates that CO~2~ does not confound the plant-valence
relationship. Future studies could extend this approach by including
volatile organic compound (VOC) measurements alongside CO~2~, which
would make it possible to assess whether other airborne chemical signals
mediate or confound the plant-emotion relationship in ways that CO~2~
alone cannot capture.

Fourth, the finding that DC-invariant, shape- and amplitude-based
features (e.g., `plant_detrend_std`, `hjorth_mobility`) consistently
outperformed level-based features provides a substantive contribution to
feature engineering in this domain and helps explain why
session-normalized features tend to yield better performance. Future
work could further investigate this pattern using more precise,
higher-resolution plant bioelectrical sensors, which may improve the
signal-to-noise ratio and reveal finer temporal dynamics than the
current AD8232-based setup permits.

## Limitations

Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the present findings.
Most fundamentally, the design of the present study did not incorporate
a ground-truth measure of emotional state against which the derived
labels could be validated. Valence and arousal labels are instead
derived from two independent proxy measures — facial expression via
HSEmotion and HRV via RMSSD, respectively — rather than from validated
psychological assessments. Because these channels are measured
independently and combined only after processing, any inaccuracy
specific to either channel propagates directly into the resulting
emotion label, without a means of cross-validation between them.

Construct validity represents a related concern. HSEmotion achieves only
approximately 65% accuracy in benchmark evaluations [@savchenko2022],
implying that a non-trivial proportion of valence labels may be
misclassified independently of any plant signal. Similarly, the arousal
axis relies exclusively on RMSSD and mean heart rate. The limitations of
these markers at lower arousal levels are well documented [@choi2017]
and are reflected in the comparatively weak arousal classification
result reported in Section 5.1.2.

The stimulus itself constitutes a further limitation. The video used to
elicit emotional responses was reused from an earlier, unrelated COIN
seminar project [@schafer2025], rather than being validated specifically
for the present study using a standardized emotion induction protocol
such as IAPS or a comparable normed stimulus set. Its capacity to
reliably elicit the intended range of valence and arousal states across
a heterogeneous participant sample was therefore not independently
confirmed.

The sample size of 15 participants, yielding 284 analyzable windows,
results in comparatively wide confidence intervals, particularly
evident in the arousal classification result discussed in
Section 5.1.2. This limits the statistical power to detect smaller
effects and constrains the precision of the reported effect size
estimates. Relatedly, the correlation analysis in Section 5.2 evaluated
22 plant-derived features across two complementary analysis variants,
without applying a correction for multiple comparisons. This should be
taken into account when interpreting the reported significance levels.

The experimental setup itself imposes additional constraints. As in
@gloor2025, a single plant species (*Kalanchoe*) was used throughout all
recording sessions. Consequently, the extent to which the observed
plant-valence association generalizes across different plant species or
individual specimens remains untested. Unlike @gloor2025, the present
study did not include sham or shielding controls, such as electrodes
attached to a non-living conductor or recordings inside a Faraday cage,
to rule out the possibility that classification performance is partly
driven by electromagnetic artifacts rather than genuine plant
physiology. Furthermore, all sessions were conducted on a single day in
a room that was not otherwise isolated from external environmental
influences. While this ensured that broad conditions such as outdoor
weather remained comparatively constant across sessions, factors such as
room temperature, humidity, and air movement were neither held constant
nor systematically recorded. Their precise influence on the plant signal
therefore cannot be determined from the present data.
